newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian govt plans for future, Yeltsin to move.
newsitem.headline: Russian govt plans for future, Yeltsin to move.

text.p: The Russian government, seeking a political consensus as Boris Yeltsin readies his comeback from illness, agreed a broad economic plan on Thursday to transform crisis into growth during the president's four-year term.

"This is the fundamental, basic, main document around which our whole economic universe will spin," Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin told the cabinet. But details of how to achieve the planned economic growth have yet to be worked out.
"It should be a direct continuation and realisation of the ideas and policies of President Boris Yeltsin's four-year election campaign programme," Itar-Tass news agency quoted Chernomyrdin as saying.

Chernomyrdin, who was flying to Minsk on Thursday evening to help resolve the political crisis in the former Soviet republic of Belarus, also chaired the first meeting of Russia's new cross-party Consultative Council set up by Yeltsin to draw communists and other opposition groups into policy-making.
The leader of the communists stayed away.
The president's press service said Yeltsin would leave hospital on Friday for the Barvikha sanatorium outside Moscow, two and a half weeks after a quintuple heart bypass operation.
Yeltsin, who said in his first television appearance on Wednesday that he felt fighting fit, could be back at work in the Kremlin by the end of the year, a spokesman said.
But the head of his medical staff warned that Yeltsin risked overdoing things by appearing on television.

The depth of the economic crisis Yeltsin will face on his return was underlined by news of an alarming fuel shortage in the Pacific city of Vladivostok and word of "difficult" talks with the International Monetary Fund on releasing loan monies.

Chernomyrdin, prime minister for four years, appeared to admit weaknesses in policy which have left millions in deep poverty and prompted more than 40 percent of voters to back Yeltsin's communist opponent in July's presidential election.
The medium-term policy from 1997 to 2000, could be more significant than the dramatic free market reforms of the past four years, Chernomyrdin was quoted as telling the cabinet.
"This is the transition to real economic growth, not just words, and real structural rebuilding, not just on paper."
The prime minister said the aim of the programme was "economic growth through social accord and consolidation".

But Yeltsin's election opponent, communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, refused to attend the first Consultative Council -- in protest, he said, at the presence of Anatoly Chubais, the Kremlin chief-of-staff who stood in for Yeltsin.
Communists were represented by lower house speaker Gennady Seleznyov. Seleznyov dropped objections to sitting with Chubais, whom the opposition say has usurped power in Yeltsin's absence.

The council discussed the peace process in breakaway Chechnya and the political crisis in Belarus, where an increasingly concerned Moscow is trying to mediate between President Alexander Lukashenko and the Minsk parliament.
There were signs, however, that the Russian opposition is not about to give the convalescing president an easy ride.
Zyuganov said Yeltsin may not be able up to tackling Russia's many problems even when he returns to the Kremlin.

"Anyone who knows anything about medicine knows that after three heart attacks, five bypasses and with concerns about a number of other organs, a person cannot work at full strength," the communist leader told reporters.
